title: Observability Setup
summary: Adds metrics, traces and structured logs to a service, then builds the alerts and dashboards you need to find a problem within minutes.
description: Instrumentation added late tends to be noisy and still miss the failure you care about. This skill starts with the questions you will ask during an incident, such as is it up, is it slow, is it erroring and which dependency, and instruments only what answers them.
The agent uses OpenTelemetry where the language supports it, keeps metric labels low-cardinality, and ties logs to traces so one request can be followed across services.
useWhen: A service goes to production with only console.log for visibility
An incident took hours because nobody could see which dependency was slow
Dashboards exist but nobody trusts or reads them
You are adopting OpenTelemetry in an existing service
body:
# Observability setup

Instrument to answer incident questions, not to collect everything.

## Steps

1. Read the service entry points, dependencies (databases, HTTP clients, queues) and any existing logging or metrics code.
2. Metrics: record the RED set for each endpoint or consumer: request rate, error rate and a duration histogram. Add saturation signals such as queue depth, pool usage and memory. Allowed labels: route template, method, status class. Never label by user ID, URL with IDs, or error message.
3. Traces: add OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation, then manual spans around business operations. Propagate the W3C `traceparent` header on outgoing calls. Sample sensibly: keep errors and slow traces.
4. Logs: emit one JSON object per line with `timestamp`, `level`, `service`, `trace_id`, `span_id` and a stable `event` name. Log decisions and failures, not every function call. Redact tokens, passwords and personal data.
5. Alerts: alert on symptoms users feel (error ratio, latency percentile, no traffic), with a runbook link and an owner. Do not alert on CPU alone.
6. Dashboards: one overview with rate, errors and latency on top, dependencies below. Use the same time range on every panel.
7. Verify locally: run the service, send a request, and confirm the span, metric and log line appear with the same trace ID.

## Rules

- Never send telemetry to an endpoint the user did not name.
- Never add high-cardinality labels.

## Report

What is instrumented, metric names, alert rules with thresholds, and how to see a request end to end.

example.prompt: Add observability to our checkout service
example.result: Added OpenTelemetry tracing with spans for payment and inventory calls, http_server_duration and http_server_errors metrics by route, JSON logs with trace_id, and two alerts: 5xx ratio above 2 percent for 5 minutes, p95 above 800 ms for 10 minutes. Verified one request shows the same trace_id in span and log.

faq.question: Which backend does it assume?
faq.answer: None. It emits OpenTelemetry data, so you can point it at Grafana, Datadog, Honeycomb or a local collector by changing the exporter setting.

faq.question: Will it slow my service?
faq.answer: Overhead is small with batching and sampling, and the skill checks request latency before and after to confirm it.

access: Reads service code and edits it to add instrumentation
Runs the service and tests locally; sends telemetry only to the collector you configure
